title: Public Engagement Is a Procurement Market, Not an Event Calendar
subtitle: Hong Kong does not have a public engagement problem — it has a procurement one. The Information Services Department’s 2026-27 budget is HK$651.1 million, and in 2025 the department assisted 680 public events across television, radio, digital, print, outdoor advertising and on-site activity. Election publicity alone carried a HK$177 million allocation. The money is real, the calendar is full, and the formats already exist. What is missing is the layer that decides whether any of it changes behaviour: the design of the moment a citizen actually decides. Look at what government buys and the gap becomes visible — exhibition design, build and maintenance awards at the City Gallery alone have run from HK$7.96 million to HK$19.79 million, bought as production rather than as strategy with measurement attached. That is the least served, most measurable part of public engagement in this city, and it is the part we work on.

title: Strategic Nudges: Small Prompts, Measurable Behaviour
subtitle: The best nudge is not a louder message — it is a better-designed choice at the moment of decision. That one line separates two entirely different ways of changing behaviour. The loud way keeps adding pressure: more reminders, more urgency, more noise, all of it trying to change what people want. The designed way changes the decision itself — the form placed in their hand, the default already ticked, the sign standing exactly where they hesitate, the object given at the second it is needed. Nothing is demanded of anyone's willpower, and nothing has to be taken away from the experience. The right choice simply becomes easier to make than to avoid. Which is why the numbers on this page are not a story about persuasion. They are a story about design.
